summary: Gives requirements on IPng from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture described in RFC 1322. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A list of what the next Internet design must support so that data can be steered across many networks efficiently.

subtitle: What the next Internet design must support for scalable routing

tldr.problem: IPv4 is running out of addresses, and the next IP version (IPng) needs to support highly scalable routing across the global Internet. The routing architecture needs clear requirements.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists six key requirements from the perspective of the Unified Routing Architecture: topologically significant addressing, flexible hierarchy, full hierarchical addresses in headers, support for both hierarchical and non-hierarchical routing, routing labels (strong and weak), and flexible source routing.
tldr.outcome: These requirements influenced the design of IPv6 and modern routing systems. The focus on scalable hierarchical routing and flexible source route options shaped the next generation of Internet protocols.

today: IPv6, which ultimately replaced IPv4, incorporated many of these routing principles. The emphasis on scalable hierarchical addressing and flexible routing options has remained central to modern routing architecture.

sections.title: Requirements for Scalable Routing
sections.content:
This RFC responds to a call for criteria for the next Internet Protocol (IPng) with requirements from the Unified Routing Architecture perspective. As IPv4 addresses become scarce and the Internet grows, the routing system must support much larger scales while remaining efficient.

Six core requirements are presented, each addressing a different aspect of routing scalability: how addresses should be structured, how routing information should be organized, how packets should carry routing information, and how the system should handle special cases like source-specified routes.
sections.eli5: As the Internet grows bigger, routers need smarter ways to find where to send packets. Here are six important rules the new design should follow.

sections.title: The Six Key Requirements
sections.content:
Requirement 1: IPng addressing must support topologically significant address assignment, enabling scalable routing based on address structure.

Requirement 2: Addressing must not impose fixed levels of hierarchy. Different parts of the network topology may need different numbers of hierarchy levels, and these levels must not be statically tied to address fields.

Requirement 3: Hop-by-hop forwarding requires the packet header to carry enough information to determine the next hop unambiguously. Unless context-sensitive forwarding is defined, the header must include the full hierarchical destination address.

Requirement 4: Hierarchical addressing should not mandate strictly hierarchical routing. The system must support both hierarchical and non-hierarchical (policy-based) routes.

Requirement 5: Packets should carry a "routing label" or "route ID" to identify which Forwarding Information Base (FIB) to use. Two types should be supported: "strong" labels (packet is discarded if the label is not found) and "weak" labels (fallback to default FIB based on destination address).

Requirement 6: Source routing must support individual routers or groups of routers, subnet constraints, flexible default behavior when routes fail, and mechanisms to verify route feasibility.
sections.eli5: The address must match the network shape, routers need enough information in each packet, and there must be ways to override normal routing when needed.

sections.title: Context and Impact
sections.content:
This RFC was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550, which called for various criteria and white papers on IPng proposals. The publication here does not imply the IPng area's acceptance of all ideas, but rather documents one architecture's perspective on what IPng must support.

The requirements reflect the thinking of researchers from USC, Cisco Systems, and IBM's Watson Research Center as the Internet engineering community debated how to replace IPv4 while meeting diverse routing needs.
sections.eli5: This is one expert team's opinion on what IPng needs, sent to the people deciding on the next Internet design.

references.text: Estrin, D., "Unified Routing Architecture", RFC 1322, May 1992.
RFC 1550 is referenced as the call for criteria.
